clue.text: Steward well-known by Edgar for what he was

definitions.meaning: the household servant of Goneril in King Lear

definitions.text: well-known by Edgar for what he was
definitions.meaning: in King Lear Edgar tells this man 'I know thee well: a serviceable villain'

explanation.surface: A steward whom Edgar knew well for the kind of man he was.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's King Lear, Goneril's steward is killed by Edgar, who greets him with 'I know thee well'.
explanation.definitionFit: The character is the scheming servant who runs Goneril's household in the play.

clue.text: Lean Trollopean chaplain

definitions.meaning: to lean is to tilt or incline
Obadiah, the bishop's oily chaplain in Trollope's Barchester Towers

explanation.surface: A thin clergyman out of a Trollope novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lean' looks like an adjective describing the chaplain, but it is a verb meaning incline.
explanation.definitionFit: To incline or tilt is a verb synonym; the chaplain is a character in Barchester Towers.

clue.text: Seen in church, but said to be opposed to singing

indicators.note: said signals that the phrase before it is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: against the choir, so anti-choir

explanation.surface: Something found in church that seems hostile to the music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said to be' turns ANTI-CHOIR into its sound-alike, the space before the choir in a church.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the vestibule or area in front of the choir stalls, a feature of church buildings.

clue.text: Political economy is such a science, thought Carlyle

definitions.text: Political economy is such a science, thought Carlyle

parts.words: Political economy is such a science, thought Carlyle
parts.note: Thomas Carlyle famously called economics a gloomy science in an 1849 essay

explanation.surface: Carlyle's opinion of what sort of science economics is.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlyle's coinage 'the ___ science' described economics as gloomy and depressing.

clue.text: His head of state was barely visible

definitions.text: His head of state was barely visible

parts.words: His head of state was barely visible
parts.note: the Danish author's fairy tale about an emperor parading in clothes that do not exist, so he is in fact naked

explanation.surface: A monarch who could hardly be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barely' means scarcely, but also hints that the emperor was bare: The Emperor's New Clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish storyteller wrote The Emperor's New Clothes, whose ruler walks out naked.

clue.text: Itinerant preacher as murderee in Sand bourne

definitions.text: Itinerant preacher as murderee in Sand bourne

parts.words: Itinerant preacher as murderee in Sand bourne
parts.note: Tess's seducer in Hardy's novel turns wandering preacher and is later stabbed by her at Sandbourne

explanation.surface: A travelling preacher murdered at a seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandbourne (printed split as 'Sand bourne') is Hardy's name for Bournemouth, where Tess kills her seducer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's villain in Tess of the d'Urbervilles briefly becomes a wandering evangelist before being murdered.

clue.text: Poet misled Wilde, say

indicators.note: misled means led astray, so the letters are sent out of order

explanation.surface: A poet who led Oscar Wilde astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misled' rearranges WILDE SAY; Cecil Day-Lewis was Poet Laureate from 1968.
explanation.definitionFit: Cecil Day-Lewis was an Anglo-Irish writer of verse and Poet Laureate.

clue.text: Sort of stuff offered by Hay and Wolfe

definitions.text: Sort of stuff offered by Hay and Wolfe

parts.words: Sort of stuff offered by Hay and Wolfe
parts.note: Ian Hay's 1908 novel and Tom Wolfe's 1979 book about astronauts share the title The ___ Stuff

explanation.surface: Two writers both supplying some kind of material.
explanation.definitionFit: Both books are titled with this word before 'Stuff', meaning the proper qualities.

clue.text: Her garden sounded relevant

parts.note: German sounds like germane, meaning relevant

explanation.surface: A woman whose garden seemed to the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounded relevant' hints at 'germane', which sounds like German, recalling Elizabeth and her German Garden (1898).
explanation.definitionFit: The narrator of von Arnim's novel is the woman whose German garden gives the book its title.

clue.text: Poor verse, or libretti for bad operettas, at the end of the day

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters are spoilt and rearranged
at the end of picks out the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Weak verse, like the libretti written for bad operettas, at the end of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges OPERETTAS; 'at the end of' takes Y from 'day'. 'or libretti for' is padding that fits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetaster is an inferior poet, and his output is weak, worthless versifying.

clue.text: The Raven, from Dickens

parts.note: the talking pet bird in Barnaby Rudge, not Poe's poem

explanation.surface: The Raven, apparently written by Dickens rather than Poe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Raven' suggests Poe's poem, but this is the raven kept by Barnaby in Dickens's Barnaby Rudge.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnaby's pet raven in Dickens's novel bears this name.

clue.text: Some chablis, then chardonnay, for Dorset mayor

indicators.note: some means only a part of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: A Dorset mayor choosing some wines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' signals letters lying inside 'then chardonnay'. Michael Henchard is Hardy's Mayor of Casterbridge (Dorchester, in Dorset).
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Henchard is the title character of Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge, set in Dorset.

clue.text: Additional charges for very minor characters

definitions.meaning: film or stage walk-on actors with no lines

explanation.surface: Surcharges levied on bit-part actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are senses of the word for supplements: added costs, and background performers.

clue.text: African Queen achieved nothing

parts.note: achieved means did, past tense
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: The African Queen never got anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'African Queen' suggests the film, but this is the queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid.
explanation.definitionFit: The founder-queen of Carthage, in north Africa, abandoned by Aeneas.

clue.text: Blake's night flier

parts.note: in Blake's The Sick Rose a worm that cannot be seen flies in the night

explanation.surface: A nocturnal creature from Blake.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake's worm 'That flies in the night' is described as unseen.

clue.text: Duke of Anjou to rule (that is, king)

parts.note: to rule is to reign
IE is the abbreviation of id est, that is
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A French duke given power to rule.
explanation.walkthrough: Reignier, Duke of Anjou and titular King of Naples, appears in Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 1.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Reignier is the French nobleman holding this ducal title in Henry VI Part 1.

clue.text: He got icon wrong in rationalist building style

indicators.note: wrong means put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man mistaken about an icon in a rationalist architectural style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges HE GOT ICON. 'in rationalist' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Neo-Gothic is the revived medieval architectural manner of the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Boorish cavalry officer from Victorian fiction, said to be from Northern Ireland

definitions.text: Boorish cavalry officer from Victorian fiction

indicators.note: said signals that the phrase is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a Derry man comes from Derry, a city in Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: An uncouth Victorian cavalryman reputedly from Ulster.
explanation.walkthrough: Festus Derriman is the bullying yeomanry officer in Hardy's The Trumpet-Major (1880).
explanation.definitionFit: Festus is the loutish yeoman soldier in Hardy's novel The Trumpet-Major.

clue.text: Hardy farmer James, always with strange need!

parts.note: always means ever

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters are made odd by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A Hardy farmer forever finding odd needs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges NEED into DENE. In Far from the Madding Crowd Bathsheba inherits the farm of her uncle James.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathsheba's uncle James, the farmer in Far from the Madding Crowd, shares her surname.

clue.text: Strauss's old lecher said to be bovine

indicators.note: said signals that the word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a bovine animal is an ox

explanation.surface: An elderly Strauss womaniser reputedly like a bull.
explanation.walkthrough: Baron Ochs is the boorish elderly suitor in Strauss's opera Der Rosenkavalier.
explanation.definitionFit: Baron Ochs auf Lerchenau is the lecherous older nobleman in Der Rosenkavalier.

clue.text: He … running into the house, exposed his back and — to the whole family" (Smollett, Humphrey Clinker)

definitions.text: He … running into the house, exposed his back and — to the whole family" (Smollett, Humphrey Clinker)

parts.words: He … running into the house, exposed his back and — to the whole family" (Smollett, Humphrey Clinker)
parts.note: the missing word in Smollett's sentence is an old jocular term for the head

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from Smollett's Humphry Clinker.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash stands for an old slang word for the head, which also means a candle bracket.
explanation.definitionFit: In old slang the word means a person's head, here exposed along with his back.

clue.text: A dams heroine gets these wrong, right afterwards

indicators.note: afterwards places the next piece after the anagram
wrong signals that the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: An Adams heroine gets these things wrong, and right after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A dams' is Adams, printed with a space: Henry Adams's 1884 novel Esther. 'wrong' rearranges THESE into ESTHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is the title heroine of Henry Adams's novel, published under a pseudonym.

clue.text: Freeman portrayed its highway

parts.note: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman's 1900 novel The ___'s Highway

explanation.surface: A man named Freeman depicted a road.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Wilkins Freeman's historical romance is titled after this organ's highway.

clue.text: Jean Plaidy's was victorious

parts.note: Jean Plaidy's novel about the Queen is titled with her name followed by 'Victorious'

explanation.surface: A Jean Plaidy character who triumphed.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaidy's 1985 novel tells the life of this nineteenth-century British queen.

clue.text: Paul Theroux saw more than fifty happy ones paddling the Pacific

definitions.text: Paul Theroux saw more than fifty happy ones paddling the Pacific

parts.words: Paul Theroux saw more than fifty happy ones paddling the Pacific
parts.note: Theroux's kayaking travel book The Happy ___ of Oceania: Paddling the Pacific

explanation.surface: Theroux kayaked past dozens of cheerful places in the Pacific.
explanation.definitionFit: Theroux's book visits many happy islands of Oceania by kayak.

clue.text: Singers perceived — the scheme of this verse, is easy to see, and that may well be for better or worse

definitions.meaning: the clue's lines end verse, see, be, worse: outer lines rhyme with each other, inner lines likewise

explanation.surface: A rhyming clue whose pattern is plain, for better or worse.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is itself a little poem whose four lines rhyme in the pattern it describes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish quartet; also the rhyme pattern where first and fourth lines rhyme, enclosing the middle pair.

clue.text: Humour of Burton

definitions.meaning: one of the four bodily humours, black bile
Robert Burton wrote The Anatomy of ___ (1621)

explanation.surface: A joke by Burton.
explanation.definitionFit: Black bile was a humour of medieval medicine, and Burton anatomised the gloom it caused.

clue.text: "Politic, cautious, and meticulous; / Full of high —, but a bit obtuse." (T. S. Eliot)

definitions.text: "Politic, cautious, and meticulous; / Full of high —, but a bit obtuse." (T. S. Eliot)

parts.words: "Politic, cautious, and meticulous; / Full of high —, but a bit obtuse." (T. S. Eliot)
parts.note: the missing word in Prufrock means lofty maxims or opinions

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from Eliot's Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock.
explanation.definitionFit: In the older sense the word means sententious, maxim-laden talk, which Prufrock's attendant lord is full of.

clue.text: Orsino would have had it of music

definitions.text: Orsino would have had it of music

parts.words: Orsino would have had it of music
parts.note: the Duke opens Twelfth Night with 'If music be the food of love, play on; Give me ___ of it'

explanation.surface: What Duke Orsino wanted from music.
explanation.definitionFit: Orsino asks for a surfeit of music so that his appetite for love may sicken.
